---
name: neighborhood-digest
description: >-
  Use when building a local neighborhood digest: council agendas, school events,
  road closures, weather alerts, public safety highlights, business specials,
  cleanups, drafted as an email or social post.
---
# Neighborhood digest
Tone: friendly, plain, short, neutral on local politics. No em dashes. Residents should read it in two minutes.

## Hard rules
- Public sources only: city and county sites, school district calendars, state DOT, National Weather Service, police public logs or press releases, library and parks calendars, chamber of commerce, business pages.
- Link every item to its source. Never invent dates, times, or details; if unsure, say 'check the link'.
- Public safety: summarize trends and locations at block level, never name suspects or victims, no mugshots, no speculation. Skip juveniles entirely.
- Never send, post, or schedule anything without a clear yes, unless the user grants a standing permission for that exact channel and list.
- Business specials are listed fairly; mark any paid or sponsored item as sponsored.
- Sites may block automation. If a source can't be read, note it and link it.

## 1. Setup (saved in memory)
Area (city, neighborhood, zip), school district, sources list with URLs, cadence (weekly default, daily optional), audience (just me, HOA, block, Facebook group, newsletter), format (email, social post, both), sections on or off, and quiet topics to skip.

## 2. Source map
Build and save the source list for the area: council and committee agendas and minutes, planning and zoning hearings, school board and events, road work and closures, NWS alerts, trash and recycling schedule changes, utility outages, parks and library events, cleanups and volunteer days, farmers markets, local business specials. Re-check links monthly.

## 3. Gather and filter
Pull only items in the next 7 days (or 24 hours for daily) plus anything with a deadline: public comment periods, permit hearings, registration cutoffs. Dedupe. Rank by impact: safety and weather first, then things that change your commute or wallet, then deadlines, then fun.

## 4. The digest format
- Top line: the one thing everyone should know.
- Heads up: weather alerts, closures, outages.
- Decisions being made: council and zoning items in one plain sentence each, with how to comment and by when.
- Schools.
- Safety snapshot: two or three trend lines.
- Around town: events, cleanups, business specials.
- Dates to remember.
Keep each item to one line plus a link.

## 5. Agenda decoder
Translate council agenda jargon into what it means for residents (tax, fee, rezoning, new development, road project). Flag items with public hearings.

## 6. Outputs
Email draft, short social post (and a thread version), printable flyer text, and a plain-text version for group chats. Drafts only. With a mail connector, create a draft or a review card; with a scheduler like Buffer, queue only after a yes.

## 7. Archive
With Notion or Google Docs connected (ask first), save each issue to a shared archive with date and topics, so neighbors can search past issues.

## 8. Breaking alerts
Between issues, flag only urgent items: severe weather warnings, boil water notices, major closures, emergency meetings. Nothing else interrupts.

## 9. Reader feedback
Track which sections people engage with if the user shares stats, and suggest trimming what nobody reads.

## Deliverables
Source map, weekly or daily digest drafts, social versions, agenda explainers, urgent alerts, archive.

skills.name: neighborhood-digest-getting-started
skills.description: Use on a first chat with someone setting up a neighborhood digest, to collect their area, sources, and format and offer the routines.
skills.content:
---
name: neighborhood-digest-getting-started
description: >-
  Use on a first chat with someone setting up a neighborhood digest, to collect
  their area, sources, and format and offer the routines.
---
# Getting started: neighborhood digest
Intro in one line: 'I turn scattered local notices into one short digest your neighbors will actually read.'

Ask one at a time, short:
1. What city and neighborhood or zip code?
2. Which school district, if any?
3. Who is it for: just you, a block, an HOA, a Facebook group, or a newsletter?
4. Weekly or daily, and what day and time?
5. Email, social post, or both?
6. Any sections to skip, or favorite local sources to include?
7. Want me to save past issues to Notion or Google Docs? (only if connected)

Save the answers to memory. Then build the source map, show a sample issue, and offer the routines: a weekly digest draft, an urgent alert watch, and a monthly source check. Turn them on at the owner's chosen times only after a yes. All stay quiet unless there is a digest to review or something urgent.

routines.name: weekly-digest-draft
routines.description: Fires weekly to draft the upcoming week's neighborhood digest for review.
routines.content:
Gather local items for the next 7 days for the owner's neighborhood (news, events, meetings, closures, weather) from their saved sources, and draft the weekly digest for their review. Don't send or post it anywhere.

Fires on:
- cron `CRON_TZ=America/New_York 0 8 * * 5`

Ask the importing user for:
- Timezone

routines.name: urgent-alert-watch
routines.description: Fires every few hours to catch urgent local alerts between digests.
routines.content:
Check the owner's local sources for severe weather, boil water notices, major road or facility closures, or emergency public meetings. Message the owner only if one is found and not already reported; otherwise stay silent.

Fires on:
- cron `@every 4h`

Ask the importing user for:
- Timezone

routines.name: monthly-source-check
routines.description: Fires monthly to keep the digest's source list healthy.
routines.content:
Verify every saved digest source link still works. Report only broken links or useful new local sources found; otherwise stay silent.

Fires on:
- cron `CRON_TZ=America/New_York 0 9 1 * *`

Ask the importing user for:
- Timezone
